In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EDL muscle fibers are not irreversibly damaged by long‐term denaturation.
the satellite cells of long‐term (3–6 mo) denervated EDL muscles are not exhausted, but are inactivated, with a concomitant loss in proliferative capacity.
denervation of the EDL muscle for 1–2 years results in an irreversible loss of muscle mass, a loss of muscle fiber number and size and a decrease in satellite cell number.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
long‐term denervaion results in a progressive loss of muscle fibers and satellite cells, and a progressive increase in the proportion of muscle fibers containing internal nuclei.

long‐term denerved muscle is characterized by: (1) a progressive loss of muscle fibers, which is associated with a progressive decrease in fiber cross‐sectional area and a decrease in the number of satellite cells associated with the muscle fibers; (2) an increase in satellite cell proliferation, which is associated, in part, with a loss of satellite cell differentiation and a progressive loss of myonuclei; and (3) an increase in the number of myonucleated satellite cells and
the muscle fibers in long‐term denerved muscle were not as well differentiated as those in control muscle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
long‐term denerved muscle fibers are not irreversibly damaged and can be successfully restored.
the satellite cell pool in denervated muscle is not static, but rather, it changes in a dynamic manner.
satellite cells do not appear to play a significant role in the restorative capacity of the long‐term denerved muscle.
